name: Cefotaxime
executiveSummary: 3rd-generation cephalosporin. Adult **1–2 g IV every 6–8 h** (max 12 g/day; meningitis 2 g every 4–6 h). Pediatrics 100–150 mg/kg/day (meningitis 200–300 mg/kg/day). Preferred in neonates vs ceftriaxone.
indications:
## Indications

- Respiratory, urinary, intra-abdominal, skin, bone, and meningitis infections due to susceptible gram-negatives (not reliable *Pseudomonas*).
- Neonatal sepsis (with ampicillin) per protocol.

## Precautions

- Beta-lactam allergy. Adjust in renal failure.
- Better neonatal profile than ceftriaxone (less bilirubin displacement / no typical ceftriaxone–calcium interaction).

> Not first-line antipseudomonal — use ceftazidime/cefepime/pip-tazo if *Pseudomonas* is suspected.

adulto.dose: Mild–moderate: **1 g every 8–12 h**. Severe: **1–2 g every 6–8 h**. Meningitis: **2 g every 4–6 h** (max **12 g/day**).
adulto.administration: IV: reconstitute with sterile water; dilute in NS/5% dextrose; 20–60 mg/mL over 15–30 min or bolus 3–5 min (up to ~100 mg/mL). IM possible.
adulto.notes: Shorten interval in severe CNS infections.

pediatrico.dose: < 12 years: **100–150 mg/kg/day every 6–8 h**. Meningitis: **200–300 mg/kg/day every 6 h**. CF: high ranges by center. Max **12 g/day**. ≥ 12 years: as adult.

neonatal.dose: Orientative: **50 mg/kg/dose every 12 h**; meningitis **every 8 h** (adjust by PMA/PNA).
neonatal.notes: Frequent backbone with ampicillin in neonatal sepsis.

adverseEffects:
## Adverse effects

Rash, diarrhea, phlebitis, eosinophilia, ↑ transaminases, *C. difficile*, anaphylaxis.
